definition: COTSBot is a small autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) 4.5 feet (1.4 m) long, which is designed by Queensland University of Technology (QUT) to kill the very destructive crown-of-thorns starfish (Acanthaster planci) in the Great Barrier Reef off the north-east coast of Australia.
details: It identifies its target using an image-analyzing neural net to analyze what an onboard camera sees, and then lethally injects the starfish with a bile salt solution using a needle on the end of a long underslung foldable arm. COTSBot uses GPS to navigate. The first version was created in the early 2000s with an accuracy rate of about 65%. After training COTSBot with machine learning, its accuracy rate rose to 99% by 2019. COTSBot is capable of killing 200 crown-of-thorns starfish with its two liters capacity of poison. COTSBot is capable of performing about 20 runs per day, but multiple COTSBots will be necessary to significantly impact the crown of thorns starfish populations. A smaller version of COTSBot called "RangerBot" is also being developed by QUT.

explainer.lead: COTSBot is a small autonomous underwater robot built by Queensland University of Technology to protect the Great Barrier Reef from destructive crown-of-thorns starfish. It finds the starfish with camera-based image analysis and kills them by injection, offering a way to automate an otherwise difficult underwater task.

tiers.eli5: COTSBot is like an underwater guard with a camera and a syringe. It swims using GPS, spots harmful starfish in its pictures, and gives each one a lethal injection. This helps protect the Great Barrier Reef, but many robots would be needed to make a big difference to the starfish population.
tiers.practitioner: COTSBot combines GPS navigation, an onboard camera and neural-network image analysis, followed by bile-salt injection through a needle on a foldable underslung arm. Its reported accuracy rose from about 65% in the early-2000s version to 99% by 2019 after machine-learning training. A two-litre payload covers up to 200 starfish and roughly 20 runs per day are possible, but meaningful population control requires multiple vehicles.
tiers.paperLevel: COTSBot is a 1.4 m autonomous underwater vehicle that uses GPS for navigation and a neural network to analyse onboard camera images for Acanthaster planci detection, then delivers a bile-salt solution through a needle on a foldable arm. Reported target accuracy increased from approximately 65% for the first version to 99% by 2019. Its two-litre capacity is sufficient for 200 starfish, but its per-vehicle throughput means population-scale impact requires multiple COTSBots.

explainer.example: If COTSBot's camera frames a crown-of-thorns starfish and the neural network identifies it, the robot injects the starfish with bile salts. A full two-litre load can kill up to 200 starfish.

explainer.intuition: COTSBot turns starfish control into an automated sequence: navigate underwater, recognise the target in camera images, and deliver a lethal injection.
howItWorks: The 1.4-metre autonomous underwater vehicle navigates using GPS.
Its onboard camera captures images of what is in front of it.
An image-analysing neural network examines those images to identify crown-of-thorns starfish.
After identifying a target, COTSBot uses a needle on its long, foldable underslung arm to inject a lethal bile-salt solution.
explainer.whyItMatters: Crown-of-thorns starfish are highly destructive to the Great Barrier Reef, and COTSBot automates their detection and lethal treatment. Its limited per-robot reach also shows why several vehicles would be needed for a significant population-level effect.
misconceptions: COTSBot does not collect or relocate starfish; it kills them by injection.
Its 99% reported accuracy does not mean one robot can control the reef's starfish population.
RangerBot is a smaller version under development, not simply another name for COTSBot.
